What DHS told Congress, against what happened

External findings from GAO, DHS's own Inspector General, and congressional testimony — cross-checked against the OPM workforce data in this report wherever the two overlap. One card below (OIG-25-38) is verified against the primary PDF directly; the rest trace to news reporting on underlying documents not yet independently pulled — treat those as well-sourced but not yet primary-verified.

DHS OIG, Jan 2026

CTMS "has not met its original goal to help recruit thousands of cyber experts," with only several hundred hired since 2021 launch — against an original estimate of 2,000 hires.

FEDagent, Jan 29 2026 →
Hysen testimony, Jun 26 2024

DHS CIO, House Homeland Security Committee: "We are pushing to aggressively expand CTMS." Also: "our initial rate of hires have not met our aggressive targets."

Primary source: full testimony PDF →
Appropriations

$49M (FY16–20) design/build funding, plus $93.2M enacted Mar 15, 2022 (Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2022) to launch hiring for 65 positions. A House Homeland Security member has separately referenced Congress rescinding ~$53M over slow CISA hiring — that specific rescission's date/citation is not yet pinned to primary text.

Federal News Network, Jun 2024 →
A claim worth watching

DHS publicly cited a "94% two-year retention rate" in mid-2024.

Cross-checked using maturity-eligible individual timelines in this report
Primary-verified: OIG-25-38, Sep 11 2025

A related-but-separate program: CISA "did not properly design, implement, comply with, or manage" its Cybersecurity Retention Incentive (CRI) — $138M paid FY2020–24, incentives given to ineligible staff, no recipient records kept, $1.41M in improper back-payments to 348 people. CISA has said (per press reporting, not this PDF) it's ending CRI specifically because CTMS is meant to absorb that function — this report doesn't independently confirm that transition claim.

Primary source: full OIG report PDF →
Context for 2025's decline

CISA's Sep–Oct 2025 exit wave in this report's own data is part of something much larger and independently reported: CISA's total workforce fell to ~2,400 by Dec 2025 (down ~29% since early 2025), following DOGE-driven contract cancellations (300+ election-security and red-team staff cut in Mar 2025) and mass departures — Axios reported a third of CISA's top cyber talent gone by Jun 2025.

Axios, Jun 3 2025 →

Pay raises, year by year

Each January cycle's individual pay change, person by person. Bars are exact percentage-change amounts — real administrative tiers, not a smoothed distribution. Click any bar to see exactly who got that raise.

Within-tier pay compression

Does the size of a person's raise correlate with where they already sat in their rate tier's pay range? Tested against two more mundane explanations first: a concurrent rate-tier/pay-plan change landing the same month (too few people, ~2/year, to explain the spread), and duty-station variation (people in the same city still show wide spread from 2024 on, so it isn't locality tables moving unevenly either). DC pay plan only — DL's per-tier samples are too thin to read a slope from. Each dot is one person; the line is the fitted trend across all DC people that year.

2023 shows no relationship at all — essentially everyone got the same flat percentage regardless of where they sat in their tier. Starting in 2024, that flips: people lower in their tier's range consistently got bigger raises than people near the top, and by 2025 the top of several tiers isn't just getting smaller raises — a meaningful share got exactly 0%, most sharply in RATE 05 (5 of the top 7 people that year). That's consistent with a real ceiling, not just easing off. Two readings fit the data equally well and can't be told apart without a performance-rating field OPM's public data doesn't include: either a genuine cap on what a top-of-tier person can be paid without an administrative tier promotion — plausible, since CTMS positions are paid under 6 U.S.C. 658 and DHS's own public materials only ever post "typical starting" ranges per level, never a stated ceiling — or high performers stuck at a tier's practical max going unrewarded until their next promotion. Both look identical in pay data alone.

What this report does not claim

Observed salary differences are not labeled as locality supplements. The public OPM fields used here do not isolate whether, or by how much, a CTMS-specific talent-market adjustment contributed to an individual's reported annualized adjusted basic pay. A defensible estimate would require a publicly citable schedule or an employee-level field that separates the adjustment from other pay determinants.

Methodology & caveats

Source. OPM's public open-data API (data.opm.gov), monthly employment / accessions / separations snapshots, no authentication required. Population = pay plan DC or DL intersected with the known DHS-only cybersecurity occupational-series family. The updater audits every DC/DL record by series and warns if another code appears.

DHS-CS context. The employee population uses DC/DL records in the DHS-only cybersecurity series family (2212, 2213, 2218, 2221, 2224–2226, 2228–2230). Current opportunities, technical capabilities, career tracks, and application guidance are available at the official DHS Cybersecurity Service portal.

First observed is not an exact CTMS start date. service_computation_date_leave is total creditable federal service and can predate CTMS by years. The report's cohort month is the first monthly snapshot in which a person appears in the CTMS-filtered population. Except for the left-censored first month of the dataset, that means the person appeared sometime after the preceding snapshot and by the current snapshot; it does not establish the precise appointment date. Cohort, observed-span, and retention calculations use this first-observed month.

Salary cost is estimated from observed tenure. Each employment snapshot contributes one person-month valued at one-twelfth of that record's annualized_adjusted_basic_pay. Summing those person-months estimates the salary represented while people were observed in CTMS. It is not a payroll-ledger total: the monthly data cannot resolve partial first or last months, and the estimate does not add benefits, bonuses, unpaid time, or amounts not included in that OPM pay field.

Individual tracking is inferred, not exact. The public data carries no employee ID. Each record is keyed on service computation date + duty station + age bracket + education level — unique within a single month, but the same real person can drift across that key (an age bracket ticks over, a relocation, a degree finished). A linking pass reconnects drifted records when they share a service date, the same subelement, and no more than one other field differs, while refusing to merge records whose active months overlap (concurrent people, not one person). Two different people can share a service-computation date by coincidence — CTMS hires in cohorts, so a whole batch can start the same day — so single-field matches on service date alone are deliberately not merged. A second pass then checks every resulting group as a whole, not just the individual links that built it: pairwise-valid links can still chain two unrelated people together transitively through a shared intermediate record, so any group that wouldn't survive a full pairwise check gets split back into separate people rather than risk a false merge.

Reproduce it. opm_ctms_pull.py pulls the raw snapshots, ctms_track_individuals.py builds the individual timelines and events, and ctms_report_data.py rolls everything in this page up. run.py runs all three in order.
